extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, defendants sued for patent infringement, and parties considering filing or responding to Covered Business Method (CBM) review petitions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on eligibility, filing requirements, standards, procedure, and strategic considerations for the Transitional Program for Covered Business Method (CBM) patents before the PTAB under the AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Covered Business Method (CBM) patent
rubrics_metrics.description: “A covered business method patent is ‘a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a ﬁnancial product or service, except that the term does not include patents for technological inventions.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires a two-part analysis: (1) whether the patent claims involve 'the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service'; and (2) whether the patent is directed to a 'technological invention.' Legislative history indicates the definition will be construed broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part CBM eligibility analysis (financial nature and technological invention exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, determine whether the claims are used in the practice/administration/management of a financial product or service; second, determine whether the patent is a technological invention (which would exclude it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a patent is for a technological invention is determined case-by-case, considering whether the claimed subject matter as a whole recites a technological feature that is novel and unobvious over the prior art, and whether it 'solves a technical problem using a technical solution.' The Board has construed 'financial' broadly (activities financial in nature, incidental or complementary to financial activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible grounds for CBM petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any ground of invalidity can serve as basis for petition, e.g. §101, §112, and, with caveats, §§102 and 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For patents with effective filing dates prior to March 16, 2013 (first-to-invent), a petitioner relying on prior art is limited to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §102 prior art. The program evidences that §101 challenges have been used successfully in CBMs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for filing CBM petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The review may be filed any time except for when PGR is available, starting September 16, 2012; the petition itself must be filed before the CBM program sunsets on September 16, 2020.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike PGR, there is no nine-month time limit for filing a petition for review of covered business method patents. Applies to all patents regardless of issue date (subject to sunset).

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM petition fee structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing fee: $12,000 to challenge the validity of up to 20 claims and $250 per each additional claim beyond the twentieth. Post-institution fee: $18,000 for challenging up to 15 claims and $550 per each additional claim beyond the fifteenth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice note: overall cost similar to PGR. Fees apply at filing and post-institution if review is granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may bring a CBM petition (eligibility/prerequisites)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is eligible for CBM review only if the petitioner establishes: (1) petitioner has been sued for infringement of the patent in question; (2) the patent claims are directed to 'financial products or services'; and (3) the patent claims do not recite a 'technological invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO comments suggest 'sued' likely includes parties served with cease-and-desist letters. The Board construed 'sued' to encompass litigation at any stage up to final judgment on appeal; a prior trial loss did not automatically preclude a petition if appeals were pending. Additional eligibility limits in fast facts: generally any non-owner unless petitioner/real party/privy previously filed an IPR/PGR/CBM that resulted in a final written decision, or previously filed a civil action challenging validity (a counterclaim does not bar CBM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory petition content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute the petitioner must (i) identify all real parties in interest; (ii) identify all claims challenged and all grounds on which the challenge to each claim is based; and (iii) provide copies of evidence relied upon. The petition must be accompanied by a fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are mandatory statutory elements — omission risks denial for failure to meet chapter 32 requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory (rule) petition content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: By rule the petitioner must (i) identify the grounds for standing; (ii) provide a claim construction for each challenged claim; (iii) specifically explain the grounds for unpatentability; and (iv) specifically explain the relevance of evidence relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule-level requirements demand a specific, claim-by-claim showing and justification of evidence; the preliminary pleading must be sufficiently detailed to meet the 'more likely than not' threshold if not rebutted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for instituting CBM (standard for granting petition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petition for CBM must contain information that 'if not rebutted,' demonstrates that it is 'more likely than not' that at least one of the claims challenged in the petition is unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same threshold as PGR. This is a statutory threshold applied at institution, distinct from the final trial standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeding pendency and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: CBM must be completed within one year from institution of the trial (approximately up to 18 months from filing the petition), with a single six month extension available for a showing of 'good cause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maximum 6 months from filing to decision on the petition; if instituted, 12 months from institution until final written decision (plus one 6-month extension for good cause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum and decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: CBM proceedings are heard before the Patent Trials and Appeals Board (PTAB) by a panel of three technically-trained, patent-savvy judges in a single-phase trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure and case handling are the same as PGR in terms of forum and panel composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent owner preliminary response rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent owner has a right to file a preliminary response to the petition within a time period set by the Director to show why no CBM should be instituted; the owner may challenge the petitioner's standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent owner has no obligation to file a preliminary response and may inform the PTAB it does not intend to file one. Examples of standing challenges include evidence that petitioner previously filed a civil action challenging patentability or is otherwise estopped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard and claim construction during CBM
rubrics_metrics.description: The default evidentiary standard is a preponderance of the evidence. The Office will apply the broadest reasonable construction standard to CBMs, and there will be no presumption of validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preponderance is more favorable to petitioners than the 'clear and convincing' district court standard. Broadest reasonable construction (BRI) tends to favor broader claim readings for anticipation/obviousness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery scope and standard for additional discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine discovery includes cited documents, cross-examination of declaration testimony, and information inconsistent with positions advanced during the proceeding. Additional discovery may be sought by motion under a 'good cause' standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may agree to additional discovery. The 'good cause' standard for PGR/CBM is slightly lower than the 'interests-of-justice' standard used in IPR/Derivation proceedings; 'good cause' requires a specific factual reason, while 'interests-of-justice' is broader and considers totality of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-proceeding estoppel consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppel attaches upon final written decision of the PTAB and applies to arguments that were actually raised in the CBM proceeding (not to arguments that could have been raised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After final decision, the petitioner and its real party in interest may not request or maintain a proceeding before the USPTO with respect to the challenged claim or assert in civil action that the claim is invalid on any ground that the petitioner actually raised. Patent owner may not take any action inconsistent with an adverse judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal and rehearing options
rubrics_metrics.description: A dissatisfied party may appeal to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit; either party may request rehearing of the Board’s decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard appellate routes apply; rehearing before the PTAB is available as an initial step prior to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay and settlement options
rubrics_metrics.description: CBM has stay provisions that may be attractive to a defendant in a co-pending lawsuit. The parties may settle and submit a joint motion to terminate without prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CBM can be used strategically to seek a stay of district court litigation; settlements can be structured to terminate the CBM without prejudice by joint motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations for pre-AIA first-to-invent patents (prior art availability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner who challenges claims in a covered business method patent having an effective filing date prior to March 16, 2013 based on prior art will be limited to relying on prior art defined by pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction narrows available prior art for first-to-invent patents and should inform prior-art strategy in CBM petitions against pre-AIA patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical takeaways from SAP v. Versata precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB in SAP v. Versata held: (1) petitioner had demonstrated 'more likely than not' unpatentability under §101; (2) 'sued' can encompass litigation at any stage up to final judgment on appeal; (3) CBM definition construed broadly to include activities financial in nature, incidental to financial activity, or complementary to financial activity; (4) 'technological invention' exclusion was not met where claims required only generic computer/software and no specific unconventional software/equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision suggests PTAB may be amenable to instituting CBM review in borderline cases; technological invention exclusion can fail where claims merely require routine computer implementation without specific unconventional technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast facts / procedural summary to assess viability
rubrics_metrics.description: CBM petitions must allege invalidity of at least one claim involving financial product/service practice/admin/management and not directed to a technological invention; threshold 'more likely than not'; filing deadlines and fees apply; eligibility and prior-action bars apply as noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the fast facts checklist (what is challenged; grounds; threshold; when to file; who can file; fees; timeline; discovery; settlement; Board's decision standard; appeals; estoppel) as a quick intake tool to screen potential CBM candidates.
